name: Editable Gaussian Representation
text:
# Editable Gaussian Representation

Also called: Editable Gaussian, iVR-GS Gaussian

## Overview
Editable [Gaussian Representation](#5918-gaussian-based-representation.md) extends the iVR-GS framework [7018-ivr-gs-relighting-via-gaussian-primitives.md] by parameterizing each Gaussian primitive with explicit shading attributes, enabling direct manipulation of color, opacity, and lighting effects [S1]. Unlike standard 3D [Gaussian Splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md) which treats color as a static view-dependent attribute, this method decouples geometry from shading, allowing for scene recoloring and light editing by modifying specific primitive parameters rather than retraining the entire model [S1].

## How it works
**Inputs and Outputs:**
*   **Input:** Multi-view images of a scene; initial Gaussian parameters (geometry and shading); ground-truth color images for regularization [S1].
*   **Output:** A collection of $N$ editable Gaussian primitives, each defined by geometry and shading attributes, optionally compressed via [Vector Quantization (VQ)](#1870-vector-quantization-for-volumetric-radiance-fields.md) and composed into a single model [S1].

**Data Structures:**
Each editable Gaussian $i$ is parameterized with two sets of attributes [S1]:
1.  **Geometry Attributes:** mean position $\mu_i$, rotation quaternion $q_i$, scale $s_i$, opacity $o_i$, and normal $n_i$ [S1].
2.  **Shading Attributes:** offset color $\Delta c_i$, ambient coefficient $k_{ia}$, diffuse coefficient $k_{id}$, specular coefficient $k_{is}$, and shininess $\beta_i$ [S1].

A global **Palette Color** $c_p \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is maintained per basic scene [S1].

**Rendering Formula:**
The voxel color $c_v$ is expressed as $c_v = c_p + \Delta c_i$ [S1]. The final rendered color is accumulated using standard alpha [compositing](#2436-compositing.md), where the contribution of Gaussian $i$ depends on its opacity $\alpha_i$ (derived from $o_i$) and depth-based transmittance $T_i$ [S1].

**[Training and Optimization](#6838-coarse-to-fine-sparse-volume-training.md) Steps:**
1.  **Initialization:** Initialize Gaussians with geometry attributes [G]. Set the palette color $c_p$ to the mean color value of the input multi-view images [S1].
2.  **Regularization:** During optimization, apply the following loss terms alongside the standard 3DGS photometric loss [S1]:
    *   **Opacity L1 Regularization:** Encourages opacity to be low to neutralize the tendency to use more Gaussians for compact surfaces, facilitating removal [S1]. (Specific formula not provided in the sources.)
    *   **Offset Color Sparsity:** Prevents significant palette color shifts [S1]. Defined as the L1 loss of the rendered offset color map $\Delta C = \sum_{i \in N} T_i \alpha_i \Delta c_i$ [S1].
    *   **Bilateral Smoothness:** Ensures shading attributes do not change significantly in smooth-color regions [S1]. For the ambient coefficient map $K_a = \sum_{i \in N} T_i \alpha_i k_{ia}$ and ground-truth color $c_{\text{GT}}$, the loss is $L_{\text{smooth}} = \| \nabla K_a \| \exp(-\| \nabla c_{\text{GT}} \|)$ [S1]. This regularization is similarly applied to $k_d, k_s,$ and $\beta$ [S1].
3.  **Pruning:** Periodically remove low-opacity Gaussians to reduce model size, similar to base 3DGS [S1].
4.  **[Compression](#4-compression.md) & Composition:** To recover all visible parts, multiple basic iVR-GS models are composed into a single model [S1]. Before composition, VQ using k-means clustering is applied to extract a more compact form of editable Gaussians for each basic model [S1]. The exact compression ratio and compression time are not given in the sources [S1].

**Parameters:**
*   **Palette Color ($c_p$):** Fixed during training as the mean color of input images; adjustable during inference for scene recoloring [S1].
*   **Offset Color ($\Delta c$):** Added to enhance the expressiveness of $c_p$ [S1].

**Edge Cases and Pitfalls:**
*   **Compact Surfaces:** The model tends to utilize more Gaussians to reconstruct compact surfaces because color depends on the normal attribute, making opacity L1 regularization critical to neutralize this effect [S1].
*   **Palette Shifts:** Without sparsity regularization on $\Delta c$, the offset color may cause significant deviations from the intended palette [S1].

## Subtopics

### [Text-Driven Gaussian Editing](11107-text-driven-gaussian-editing.md)
[Text-Driven Gaussian Editing](#11107-text-driven-gaussian-editing.md) modifies the appearance of VolVis scenes represented by [textured Gaussian](#9528-texture-and-appearance-representation.md) primitives using natural language text prompts while preserving underlying geometry and lighting. It distinguishes itself from iterative baseline methods by employing a one-time update strategy that applies image-to-image (IP2P) editing only once on a small subset of multi-view images, significantly reducing editing time and avoiding blurriness in semi-transparent scenes. Choose this variant when text-based appearance editing is required without altering scene geometry or requiring iterative optimization.

## Operating characteristics
*   **Time Complexity:** Training time is comparable to base 3DGS with additional regularization overhead [S1].
*   **Memory Complexity:** The base model size is larger than standard 3DGS due to additional shading attributes per Gaussian, but VQ reduces the final model size [S1].
*   **Performance:** Enables real-time scene editing (recoloring, [opacity adjustment](#4020-absorption-adjustment.md), light direction) without retraining [S1].
*   **Strengths:** Explicit control over lighting and color; composability of scenes; reduced model size via pruning and VQ [S1].
*   **Limitations:** Requires multi-view input for training; complexity in managing shared codebooks for composition [S1].

## Background
The Editable Gaussian Representation was introduced in the iVR-GS paper, which proposes Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting [S1]. It builds upon the iVR-GS method which models lighting effects using the Blinn-Phong model [7018-ivr-gs-relighting-via-gaussian-primitives.md] [S1]. The method was developed to address the lack of explicit editability in standard 3DGS for volume visualization scenes [S1].
